script.opening: “Alright, doc. The A&E doctor said my blood pressure was sky high and I need to get tablets off you. So can you sort that today? I don’t want a stroke like my mam.”

facts.text: “I’d had a skinful, tripped on the kerb outside the hostel. Cut my arm. They stitched it.” No head injury, no blackout before falling, no chest pain or palpitations.
“It’s fine — bit sore. No pus, not red.” No fever.
No headaches, no blurred vision, no chest pain, no breathlessness, no weakness or numbness, no slurred speech, no blood in your urine.

“Eight cans a day. The big ones, Stella-type.” If asked about mornings: “I get the shakes when I wake up. A can sorts it. First one’s about eight.” If asked about stopping before: “I ran out once — sweating, heart racing, couldn’t sleep. Never had a fit.” No hallucinations.

facts.topic: The alcohol service (only if asked why you missed appointments)
facts.text: Look away. “I never got any letters. They must’ve gone to Larch Close — that’s my ex’s. I left in the summer.”

facts.topic: Why now (only if asked whether you want to cut down, or what matters to you)
facts.text: “My daughter, Jade — she’s having a baby in March. She said I can’t be round the baby if I’m drinking. I want to be a grandad. Properly.” Voice cracks.

“I’m in a hostel on the Eastfield estate — the council put me there six weeks ago. Shared kitchen. I’m on Universal Credit. I can’t get to you — it’s nine miles and the bus is a fiver return. I’ve no money for that.” If asked about the hospital: “The General’s just round the back of the hostel.” If asked about a pharmacy: “There’s a chemist on the parade, two minutes away.”
“I can’t afford one of them. How am I meant to do that?”
Roll-ups, about 25 a day for 35 years. Eats “crisps, pies, whatever”. No drugs.
Mam had a stroke at 60 — “couldn’t talk or walk after, died in a home.” Dad had a heart attack at 64.
“Bit low since the split. Not suicidal — I’ve got the baby to look forward to.”

Be friendly but insistent about tablets. If the doctor does not prescribe today, repeat once: “Doc, I just need a blood pressure tablet.” Accept a clear explanation. You only reveal the letters and Jade’s baby if the doctor asks about the missed appointments or about what matters to you, and you are embarrassed. If the doctor lectures you about drinking, become defensive and short.

ice.ideas: “My blood pressure’s high and tablets will fix it.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he never received the alcohol service letters because the practice still has his ex-partner’s address; he is ashamed. He wants to cut down because his daughter has said he cannot be around her baby if he is drinking. Underneath is a real fear of a stroke like his mother’s.
ice.expectations: A prescription for BP tablets today.

cues: “I don’t want a stroke like my mam.” — fear to acknowledge and use.
“I can’t get to you.” — access barriers that will sink any standard plan.
“I never got any letters.” — an out-of-date address, not disinterest.

checkpoints.text: Reviews the A&E readings in context (pain, intoxication or withdrawal), checks for symptoms of hypertensive emergency or target-organ damage, and checks the wound
Takes a full alcohol history: quantity in units, pattern, morning drinking and shakes, previous withdrawal, seizures or delirium tremens, and screens for dependence (AUDIT or similar)
Explores social circumstances: housing, address, money, travel, phone access, mood; discovers the letters went to the wrong address and what motivates him to change

Explains that BP tablets are not started on these readings and that diagnosis needs confirmation (ambulatory or home monitoring); arranges accessible confirmation — community pharmacy BP check service near the hostel or a loaned home monitor

Plans cardiovascular assessment without extra travel: bloods (U&E, HbA1c, lipids, LFTs including GGT, FBC) at the nearby hospital phlebotomy, urine ACR and ECG combined with the suture-removal visit, QRISK3 when results are in

Advises not to stop drinking suddenly, offers referral or self-referral to the alcohol service with his correct contact details, oral thiamine, smoking cessation offer, and updates his address; offers social prescriber or housing support
Acknowledges his fear of stroke and his wish to be a grandad; avoids lecturing or judgement about drinking or housing
Builds a realistic plan with him around his constraints, safety-nets (stroke, chest pain, severe headache, withdrawal fits or confusion) and agrees follow-up by phone or video

worked.txt: “Your mum’s stroke is a really good reason to take this seriously, and so am I. The problem is that blood pressure taken when you’re in pain and had a drink can be much higher than your usual. If I start tablets on that, you might end up on medicine you don’t need — or the wrong dose.”
“You don’t need to buy a machine. The chemist on your parade does free blood pressure checks for the NHS, and can fit a 24-hour monitor. Or we can lend you one.”

worked.lbl: Ask about the missed appointments without blame
worked.txt: “The alcohol service said you missed some appointments — what happened?”
“What would be different for you if you cut down?”

“Please don’t stop suddenly — with morning shakes, stopping overnight can cause fits. The alcohol team can help you cut down safely, and I’ll start a vitamin called thiamine to protect your brain and nerves.”

“When you come in to have your stitches out, the nurse can do your blood pressure, a heart tracing and a urine test at the same time — one trip. And the blood test can be done at the General, right behind the hostel.”

f.learning: A single set of raised readings in A&E, taken when someone is in pain and intoxicated or withdrawing, does not diagnose hypertension. NICE NG136 requires confirmation with ambulatory or home monitoring for clinic readings of 140/90 or above, with same-day referral for readings of 180/120 or above with signs of retinal haemorrhage, papilloedema or life-threatening symptoms. The barrier in this case is access, and the solution is local: the NHS community pharmacy blood pressure check service offers clinic and ambulatory readings for adults over 40, many practices loan home monitors, and tests can be bundled into visits he is already making. Heavy drinking raises BP and is itself a major stroke risk; at over 150 units a week with morning withdrawal symptoms he is likely dependent, so he must not stop abruptly and needs assessment for medically assisted withdrawal, with oral thiamine for a harmful drinker with poor nutrition (NICE CG100 and CG115). Missed appointments in people with insecure housing are often a systems failure — letters to an old address — and checking contact details is a concrete act of inclusion. His wish to be a grandad is the lever for change; the GP’s job is to find it and use it, not to lecture.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management (2019, updated 2026) · NICE CG115 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis, assessment and management of harmful drinking and alcohol dependence (2011) · NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications (2010, updated 2017) · NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence (2021) · NHS England — Community Pharmacy Blood Pressure Check Service (2021)
knowledge.summary: Do not diagnose hypertension from A&E readings; confirm it with accessible monitoring, assess cardiovascular risk with bundled tests, and address alcohol dependence safely — with his real address and his real motivation.

points.t: Clinic BP 140/90 to 179/119: confirm with ABPM (daytime average) or HBPM (twice daily, two readings each, for at least 4 and ideally 7 days). Stage 1: 135/85 or above; stage 2: 150/95 or above. Investigate for target-organ damage: urine ACR and dipstick for haematuria, HbA1c, U&E and eGFR, lipids, fundi, 12-lead ECG; estimate QRISK3.

BP 180/120 or above with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, or life-threatening symptoms (new confusion, chest pain, heart failure, acute kidney injury) — same-day specialist assessment. Without these, repeat and investigate promptly.

NHS Community Pharmacy Blood Pressure Check Service: clinic and ambulatory BP for adults aged 40 and over, results sent to the GP. Practice-loaned validated home monitors. Bloods at a convenient phlebotomy site. Combine tests with existing appointments (suture removal).

AUDIT 20 or above, or morning drinking to relieve withdrawal, suggests dependence. Do not advise abrupt cessation; refer for assessment and medically assisted withdrawal (community or inpatient if previous seizures or delirium tremens). Prophylactic oral thiamine for harmful or dependent drinkers who are malnourished or at risk. Usual adult dose: thiamine 100 mg three times daily (NICE CG100/SPC; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: thiamine).
Heavy drinking raises BP and stroke risk; reducing intake lowers BP within weeks. Readings during intoxication or withdrawal are unreliable.
Check and update address and phone at every contact; flag communication needs; consider letters by text or to a hostel key worker with consent; social prescribers can support housing and benefits.

The Clear pass candidate holds the line on not prescribing today while making confirmation genuinely achievable, discovers the address error and the grandchild, and plans a safe alcohol pathway without lecturing.

model.text: Hello Mr Whitfield, I’m Dr Nwosu. Can you see and hear me? Are you somewhere you can talk?
model.why: Video and privacy check — he is in a hostel

model.text: Yeah, in my room. A&E said my blood pressure’s sky high. I need the tablets — I don’t want a stroke like my mam.
I’m sorry about your mum — that must have been hard. Let’s work out what’s going on. Can you tell me what happened on the night?
Had a skinful, fell on the kerb, cut my arm.
How’s the arm? And any headaches, blurred vision, chest pain, breathlessness, weakness or numbness?
Can I ask about drinking — no judgement, it helps me get your blood pressure right. How much in a typical day? Any shakes in the morning?
model.why: Alcohol quantity and dependence, with a reason

model.text: Eight big cans. Shakes when I wake up — a can sorts it. Never had a fit.
Thanks for being straight with me. The alcohol team said you missed some appointments — what happened there?
Never got the letters. They’ll have gone to my ex’s — I’m in a hostel now, nine miles from you.
Then that’s our problem to fix, not yours. Would you want to cut down, if we got the support right?
My daughter’s having a baby in March. She says I can’t be round it if I’m drinking. I want to be a proper grandad.

That’s a brilliant reason. On blood pressure: readings when you’re in pain and had a drink can be much higher than usual, so I won’t start tablets on those alone. We need readings over a day or a week.
model.why: Clear reason for not prescribing today

model.text: Doc, I just need a blood pressure tablet. And I can’t afford a machine.

You won’t need to buy one. The chemist on your parade can check it free and fit a 24-hour monitor — or we’ll lend you one. Your bloods can be done at the General behind the hostel, and when you come for your stitches the nurse will do a heart tracing and urine test. If it is high, we start tablets straight away.

For drinking — please don’t stop suddenly, that can cause fits. I’ll refer you back to the alcohol team with your new address and mobile, and start thiamine, a vitamin that protects your brain. Cutting down will help your blood pressure too. Would you like help with smoking or with housing — we have a link worker?
model.why: Safe alcohol plan, thiamine, smoking and social support

model.text: If you get a sudden severe headache, chest pain, weakness, a droopy face or slurred speech — 999. Same if you have a fit or get confused after cutting down. I’ll call you in a week. What’s the plan in your words?
Chemist for my blood pressure, bloods at the General, stitches and heart test at yours, don’t stop drinking all at once, and you’re sorting the alcohol people with my new address.

social.t: People in temporary accommodation move often and lose letters, phones and appointments. Text reminders, hostel key workers (with consent) and an up-to-date address reduce missed care.
A £5 bus fare is a barrier on Universal Credit. Bring services to the person — pharmacy, local phlebotomy, combined appointments.

legal.t: People do not need proof of address to register or stay registered with a GP; record a correspondence address that works.
If he drives, alcohol dependence must be declared to the DVLA — ask and advise.

professional.t: Labelling people as “did not attend” without checking contact details reinforces exclusion; GMC Good Medical Practice (2024) expects fair, accessible care.

community.t: Community alcohol service (self-referral), local stop smoking service, social prescriber or link worker, hostel support worker, Alcoholics Anonymous and SMART Recovery.

redFlags: Severe headache, visual disturbance, chest pain, neurological symptoms
Previous withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens
psychosocial: Hostel 9 miles away; no travel money
core: A&E BP 164–172/100–104 while intoxicated and in pain
About 22 units a day; morning shakes

playbook.diagnosis: Raised BP in A&E, unconfirmed (possible hypertension) in a man with alcohol dependence, heavy smoking and high cardiovascular risk; missed care due to an outdated address.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your blood pressure was high in A&E, but that was when you were hurt and had been drinking. We need to check it properly — and the drinking is the biggest thing pushing your stroke risk up.”

management.reflectIce: “You want tablets because you don’t want a stroke like your mum — and I want to protect you from that too. The quickest safe way is to get proper readings this week, and to get you support with the drinking for you and for the baby.”
management.psychosocial: Update address and mobile; text reminders; link worker for housing; use the grandchild as motivation.
sharedPlan: Pharmacy BP check service (clinic plus ambulatory) on his parade, or loaned home monitor
Bloods at the hospital phlebotomy: U&E, HbA1c, lipids, LFT and GGT, FBC
Suture removal at the practice day 10: BP, ECG, urine ACR
Re-referral to the alcohol service with correct details; do not stop suddenly; thiamine
Video or phone review in 1 week; QRISK3 and treatment decision when results back
safetyNet: 999: stroke symptoms, chest pain, sudden severe headache
999 or A&E: withdrawal fit, confusion or hallucinations
Wound redness, discharge or fever — call the practice

pitfalls.intro: Two opposite failures: starting amlodipine to satisfy the request, or giving a textbook ABPM plan he cannot possibly follow.

items.fail: Prescribes antihypertensives today based on the A&E readings.
items.why: Readings during pain and intoxication are unreliable; NICE requires out-of-office confirmation; treatment without baseline bloods and ECG is unsafe.
items.fix: Explain why, and make confirmation achievable this week.

items.fail: Labels him as a non-attender and never asks why he missed the alcohol appointments.
items.why: The cause was the practice’s outdated address; the same will happen to every future letter.
items.fix: Ask without blame and update contact details during the consultation.

items.fail: Tells him to stop drinking completely from today.
items.why: With morning withdrawal symptoms, abrupt cessation risks seizures and delirium tremens.
items.fix: Advise not to stop suddenly; refer for supported withdrawal; thiamine.

Fall and wound; BP emergency screen; alcohol and dependence; missed appointments; housing; motivation.
Why not tablets today; accessible confirmation.
Bundled tests; alcohol referral with correct details; thiamine; smoking; link worker.

wordPics.clearFail: Starts amlodipine on the A&E readings, or refuses and simply says “come in for a 24-hour monitor”; no alcohol history; moralises; no safety-net.
wordPics.fail: Correctly declines to prescribe and explains ABPM, but the plan is impractical (attend the surgery several times, buy a monitor), the address problem is missed, or he is told to stop drinking immediately.
wordPics.pass: Explains why not today; arranges pharmacy or loaned monitoring; bloods locally; alcohol history with dependence recognised; do not stop suddenly; referral and thiamine; address updated; safety-net.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass delivered without judgement: finds and uses the grandchild motivation, takes ownership of the address error, bundles tests into existing visits, offers smoking and housing support, and closes with teach-back and a dated review.

avoid.dont: “I can’t give you tablets, you need a 24-hour monitor from the surgery.”
avoid.instead: “Your local chemist can do the monitor for free — two minutes from you.”
avoid.why: Solves the barrier rather than restating the guideline.

avoid.instead: “Please don’t stop suddenly — let’s get you help to cut down safely.”
avoid.why: Abrupt withdrawal is dangerous in dependence.

avoid.dont: “You missed three appointments with the alcohol team.”
avoid.instead: “What happened with the alcohol team appointments?”
avoid.why: Curious, not accusing — uncovers the address problem.
